power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Empirically Distinguishing Self-concept Clarity and facets of Negative Affectivity
table.data_collection_started: Yes, we already collected the data.
table.research_questions: Our primary research questions will be focused on the empirical distinguishability of a measure of self-concept clarity (the Self-concept Clarity Scale; SCS) and facets of neuroticism and negative affectivity (derived from the Big Five Inventory-2 [BFI-2] and the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathy-Self Report scale [HiTOP-SR]). We will examine the empirical similarity of these scales in relation to measures assessed at baseline, and from indices derived from a 15-day ambulatory assessment protocol. Our approach is primarily descriptive/exploratory, and thus we do not specify a priori hypotheses. All models used to examine specific research questions are detailed below.
table.design_dependent_variables:
The key independent variables will be Neuroticism facet scales and more clinically-oriented Distress symptom scales from the BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR, respectively, along with the SCC. The key dependent variables are listed below.

Baseline Measures

Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology Patient Reported Outcomes (HiTOP-PRO). The HiTOP-SR (Simms et al., 2023; https://www.32plab.org/hitop) is a 405-item self-report instrument that assesses psychopathology symptoms as represented in the HiTOP model (Kotov et al., 2017). The HiTOP-SR was designed to be broad but comprehensive in scope, and assesses a wide variety of psychopathology symptoms and behaviors. Participants were asked to rate how much each item applied to them in the past month. Each item was rated using a one (“Not at all”) to four (“A lot”) Likert scale. Five broad-based factor scales (e.g., Distress, Emotionality), eighty-five specific symptom scales (e.g., Affective Lability, Depressed Mood), and eleven alcohol use scales (e.g., Craving, Hazardous Use) were computed using the HiTOP-SR items.   

At the time of data collection, the 405-item version of the HiTOP-SR had not been finalized, and we employed an earlier, 495-item version of the measure. The focus of the current study will be on 5 symptom scales related to the Distress factor (from the 9-factor solution established in Mostajabi et al., 2025). These scales are Depressed Mood, Anxious Worry, Shame/Guilt, Affective Lability, and Irritability.   

Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2). The BFI-2 (Soto & John, 2017) is a 60-item self-report measure of the Big Five personality domains. Each item was rated on a one (“Disagree strongly”) to five (“Agree strongly”) Likert scale, with participants being asked to rate their agreement with a series of statements about themselves (e.g., “I am someone who is outgoing, sociable”). Items were averaged to create mean scales for each domain, as well as mean facet scales within each domain (three facet scales for each domain). For Neuroticism, the three facet scales are Anxiety, Depression, and Emotional Volatility. 

Self-concept Clarity Scale (SCC). The SCC (Campbell et al., 1996) is a 12-item self-report measure designed to assess self-concept clarity, which refers to the extent that self-beliefs are clear, internally consistent, and stable (sample item: “In general, I have a clear sense of who I am and what I am”). Participants were asked to rate their agreement with each item using a one (“Strongly Disagree”) to five (“Strongly Agree”) Likert scale. A total mean score was computed from the twelve SCC items.   

Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8). The PHQ-8 (Kroenke et al., 2009) is a brief self-report measure of depression symptoms and assesses common features of depression. The PHQ-8 was administered using eight Likert scale items ranging from zero (“Not at all”) to three (“Nearly every day”). Participants were asked to rate how much they had been bothered by each symptom (e.g., “Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless”) in the previous two weeks. A total score reflecting overall level of depression symptoms was computed by summing the eight items.

Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6). The K6 (Kessler et al., 2003) is a brief self-report measure of overall psychological distress. The K6 is comprised of six items, each rated using a zero (“None of the time”) to four (“All of the time”) Likert scale. Participants were asked to rate how often they had a particular feeling (e.g., nervous, hopeless, that everything was an effort) in the past 30 days. The total K6 score was used as an index of overall impairment, with past work demonstrating that total scores between 13-24 indicating a clinical degree of impairment (Kessler et al., 2003).  

Momentary Outcome Measures

Momentary Affect and Stress. During each random prompt, participants rated their mood using four items. Positive affect was assessed with one item (“In the past 15 minutes, how POSITIVE have you felt?”) using a zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very Positive”) sliding scale. Participants also rated negative affect with one item (“In the past 15 minutes, how NEGATIVE have you felt?”) using a one (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very Negative”) sliding scale.

In addition to rating positive and negative affect, participants rated their momentary stress (“In the past 15 minutes, how STRESSED have you felt?”). Stress was rated using a zero (“Not at all”) to ten (“Extremely”) sliding scale. 

Impulsivity. Four items were used to assess momentary impulsivity. For each item, participants were asked whether they had engaged in the impulsive behavior in the past hour using a zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very Much”) sliding scale. The four items were, “I did something on impulse”; “I did things without worrying about the consequences”; “I decided to put off something that I had to do”; “I avoided doing something despite the consequences”. 

Event-contingent Surveys (completed after an interpersonal interaction had occurred). 

Momentary Affect and Stress During Interpersonal Interactions. Affect was assessed during interpersonal interactions with the same three items. Participants’ rated their own positive affect with the item “How POSITIVE were your emotions during the interaction?” with responses from zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very positive”). Negative affect during the interaction was assessed with the item “How NEGATIVE were your emotions during the interaction?” with responses from zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very negative”). Participants also rated how stressful they perceived the interaction (“How stressful was this interaction?”).

Momentary Self-concept Clarity (MSCC). Two items were used to assess MSCC during interpersonal interactions: “During the interaction, I was true to myself” and “During the interaction, I had a clear sense of who I was.” Responses were provided on a sliding scale of 0 (“Not at all”) to 10 (“Extremely”). Previous work has shown that the two items are highly correlated on both the between-person (r=.93, p<.001) and within-person (r=.67, p<.001) levels.

table.design_dependent_variables:
The key independent variables will be Neuroticism facet scales and more clinically-oriented Distress symptom scales from the BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR, respectively, along with the SCC. The key dependent variables are listed below.

Baseline Measures

Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology Patient Reported Outcomes (HiTOP-PRO). The HiTOP-SR (Simms et al., 2023; https://www.32plab.org/hitop) is a 405-item self-report instrument that assesses psychopathology symptoms as represented in the HiTOP model (Kotov et al., 2017). The HiTOP-SR was designed to be broad but comprehensive in scope, and assesses a wide variety of psychopathology symptoms and behaviors. Participants were asked to rate how much each item applied to them in the past month. Each item was rated using a one (“Not at all”) to four (“A lot”) Likert scale. Five broad-based factor scales (e.g., Distress, Emotionality), eighty-five specific symptom scales (e.g., Affective Lability, Depressed Mood), and eleven alcohol use scales (e.g., Craving, Hazardous Use) were computed using the HiTOP-SR items.   

At the time of data collection, the 405-item version of the HiTOP-SR had not been finalized, and we employed an earlier, 495-item version of the measure. The focus of the current study will be on 5 symptom scales related to the Distress factor (from the 9-factor solution established in Mostajabi et al., 2025). These scales are Depressed Mood, Anxious Worry, Shame/Guilt, Affective Lability, and Irritability.   

Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2). The BFI-2 (Soto & John, 2017) is a 60-item self-report measure of the Big Five personality domains. Each item was rated on a one (“Disagree strongly”) to five (“Agree strongly”) Likert scale, with participants being asked to rate their agreement with a series of statements about themselves (e.g., “I am someone who is outgoing, sociable”). Items were averaged to create mean scales for each domain, as well as mean facet scales within each domain (three facet scales for each domain). For Neuroticism, the three facet scales are Anxiety, Depression, and Emotional Volatility. 

Self-concept Clarity Scale (SCC). The SCC (Campbell et al., 1996) is a 12-item self-report measure designed to assess self-concept clarity, which refers to the extent that self-beliefs are clear, internally consistent, and stable (sample item: “In general, I have a clear sense of who I am and what I am”). Participants were asked to rate their agreement with each item using a one (“Strongly Disagree”) to five (“Strongly Agree”) Likert scale. A total mean score was computed from the twelve SCC items.   

Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8). The PHQ-8 (Kroenke et al., 2009) is a brief self-report measure of depression symptoms and assesses common features of depression. The PHQ-8 was administered using eight Likert scale items ranging from zero (“Not at all”) to three (“Nearly every day”). Participants were asked to rate how much they had been bothered by each symptom (e.g., “Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless”) in the previous two weeks. A total score reflecting overall level of depression symptoms was computed by summing the eight items.

Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6). The K6 (Kessler et al., 2003) is a brief self-report measure of overall psychological distress. The K6 is comprised of six items, each rated using a zero (“None of the time”) to four (“All of the time”) Likert scale. Participants were asked to rate how often they had a particular feeling (e.g., nervous, hopeless, that everything was an effort) in the past 30 days. The total K6 score was used as an index of overall impairment, with past work demonstrating that total scores between 13-24 indicating a clinical degree of impairment (Kessler et al., 2003).  

Momentary Outcome Measures

Momentary Affect and Stress. During each random prompt, participants rated their mood using four items. Positive affect was assessed with one item (“In the past 15 minutes, how POSITIVE have you felt?”) using a zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very Positive”) sliding scale. Participants also rated negative affect with one item (“In the past 15 minutes, how NEGATIVE have you felt?”) using a one (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very Negative”) sliding scale.

In addition to rating positive and negative affect, participants rated their momentary stress (“In the past 15 minutes, how STRESSED have you felt?”). Stress was rated using a zero (“Not at all”) to ten (“Extremely”) sliding scale. 

Impulsivity. Four items were used to assess momentary impulsivity. For each item, participants were asked whether they had engaged in the impulsive behavior in the past hour using a zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very Much”) sliding scale. The four items were, “I did something on impulse”; “I did things without worrying about the consequences”; “I decided to put off something that I had to do”; “I avoided doing something despite the consequences”. 

Event-contingent Surveys (completed after an interpersonal interaction had occurred). 

Momentary Affect and Stress During Interpersonal Interactions. Affect was assessed during interpersonal interactions with the same three items. Participants’ rated their own positive affect with the item “How POSITIVE were your emotions during the interaction?” with responses from zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very positive”). Negative affect during the interaction was assessed with the item “How NEGATIVE were your emotions during the interaction?” with responses from zero (“Neutral”) to ten (“Very negative”). Participants also rated how stressful they perceived the interaction (“How stressful was this interaction?”).

Momentary Self-concept Clarity (MSCC). Two items were used to assess MSCC during interpersonal interactions: “During the interaction, I was true to myself” and “During the interaction, I had a clear sense of who I was.” Responses were provided on a sliding scale of 0 (“Not at all”) to 10 (“Extremely”). Previous work has shown that the two items are highly correlated on both the between-person (r=.93, p<.001) and within-person (r=.67, p<.001) levels.

Participants were asked to rate how often they had a particular feeling (e.g., nervous, hopeless, that everything was an effort) in the past 30 days.

info.title: Who I Am vs. How Do I Feel? Testing the Empirical Distinctiveness of Self-Concept Clarity and Trait Negative Affectivity

text.text: Low) self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity ostensibly capture distinct domains: a lack of clarity and stability of self-beliefs and the tendency to experience different kinds of negative emotions, respectively.
Despite their clear theoretical distinctions, they are strongly correlated and show overlapping nomological networks.
To date, there has not been a thorough evaluation of how facets of trait negative affectivity overlap with, and are distinct from, (low) self-concept clarity.

Using an adult sample (N=493) who completed a series of baseline questionnaires followed by a 15-day ecological momentary assessment protocol, we evaluated the similarities and differences between the Self-concept Clarity Scale (SCCS) and a comprehensive collection of trait negative affectivity facets.

Results from multilevel structural equation models indicated that the SCCS accounted for unique variance in a few select outcomes, most notably global depression and distress measures, state authenticity and rash inaction, providing evidence of unique predictive validity.

However, our findings also indicated substantial empirical overlap between the SCCS and all facets of trait negative affectivity, with nearly identical patterns of empirical relations of momentary affective outcomes.
Furthermore, much of the SCCS's relations with maladaptive functioning was accounted for by its overlap with trait negative affectivity.

Overall, our findings clarify important nuances in the empirical overlap and distinctiveness between the SCCS and facets of trait negative affectivity, and we discuss the conceptual and practical implications of this overlap for future research on personality and self-functioning.

Self-concept is conceptualized as the understanding of one's traits (e.g., work ethic, intelligence), roles (e.g., parent, manager, spouse), and values (e.g., morals, faith, spirituality) which together guide the processing and interpretation of self-relevant information (Greenwald & Pratkanis, 1984; Kihlstrom & Cantor, 1984).

text.text: These empirical findings extend to interpersonal functioning.

Higher self-concept clarity is related to lower social anxiety (Stopa et al., 2010) and reduced loneliness (Richman et al., 2016), whereas individuals with lower self-concept clarity appear less likely to engage in moral behaviors (e.g., donating to charity) and more likely to engage in antisocial behaviors (e.g., cheating and dishonesty; Wang & Touré-Tillery, 2024).

text.text: Within romantic relationships, lower selfconcept clarity is tied to difficulties in relationship formation and lower relationship satisfaction (Emery et al., 2015; Lewandowski et al., 2010).

text.text: Thus, self-concept clarity is relevant both to broader psychological functioning and to the development and maintenance of social roles and relationships.

Trait negative affectivity captures the tendency to experience unstable and unpleasant emotions and is represented in all prominent models of personality (Matthews et al., 2003; Leary & Hoyle, 2009), most notably as Neuroticism in the Five-factor Model (FFM) of personality (Gore & Widiger, 2013).

text.text: It is also the FFM domain with the strongest empirical relations with various forms of internalizing psychopathology, including anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and major depressive disorder (Clark et al., 1994; Kotov et al., 2010), but also somatoform disorders, schizophrenia, and eating pathology (Malouff et al., 2005).

text.text: Beyond psychopathology, its interpersonal correlates closely parallel those observed for self-concept clarity.

Higher trait negative affectivity is related to elevated antisocial tendencies (Vize et al., 2019), heightened social anxiety (Newby et al., 2017), and diminished satisfaction within romantic relationships (Malouff et al., 2010), whereas low levels are associated with greater marital satisfaction (Gattis et al., 2004), occupational success (Ozer & Benet-Martinez, 2006), and overall quality of life (Lynn & Steel, 2006).

text.text: Finally, trait negative affectivity has been theorized to manifest in heightened self-criticism, sensitivity to criticism from others, and feelings of personal inadequacy (Watson et al., 1994).

text.text: The overlap between trait negative affectivity and self-concept clarity also extends to personality pathology, particularly features of borderline personality disorder (BPD).
Trait negative affectivity has been identified as the FFM domain with the strongest association with BPD (Morey & Zanarini, 2000).

text.text: Relatedly, women with BPD exhibit significantly lower selfconcept clarity than healthy controls (Roepke et al., 2011).

text.text: Furthermore, interventions targeting self-concept clarity have been accompanied by marked decreases in depressive symptoms and general psychopathology (Roepke et al., 2011).

text.text: The ambiguity surrounding where trait negative affectivity ends and identity-related constructs such as self-concept clarity begin is at the forefront of ongoing debates about the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) in DSM-5.
The AMPD conceptualizes personality pathology using two complementary components.

Criterion A assesses the severity of personality dysfunction, including disturbances in identity, self-direction, and interpersonal functioning (Skodol, 2012), making the coherence and clarity of one's self-concept a central aspect of personality functioning.
text.formatted: Criterion A assesses the severity of personality dysfunction, including disturbances in identity, self-direction, and interpersonal functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Skodol, 2012)</ref>, making the coherence and clarity of one's self-concept a central aspect of personality functioning.

text.text: Criterion B pertains to the presence of maladaptive personality traits.

Although Criteria A and B were intended to capture distinct aspects of personality pathology (APA, 2013), accumulating evidence suggests that the distinction is less clear in practice, and debate continues over whether dysfunction in self and interpersonal functioning can be empirically distinguished from maladaptive traits, most notably trait negative affectivity (see Morey et al., 2022; Sleep & Lynam, 2022; Widiger et al., 2023).

text.text: Taken together, the reviewed literature highlights considerable empirical overlap between measures of self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity, despite clear conceptual distinctions between the constructs.
This overlap is particularly surprising given the strong face validity of many measures of self-concept clarity that do not explicitly reference negative emotionality.
Face validity refers to the extent to which a scale appears practical, pertinent, and related to its intended purpose (Mosier, 1947, p. 192).
text.formatted: Face validity refers to the extent to which a scale appears practical, pertinent, and related to its intended purpose <ref type="bibr">(Mosier, 1947, p. 192)</ref>.

text.text: For example, SCCS items directly assess the clarity and coherence of one's self-concept without referencing negative emotionality (e.g., "I spend a lot of time wondering about what kind of person I really am," "My beliefs about myself seem to change very frequently," "In general, I have a clear sense of who I am and what I am"; Campbell et al., 1996).

text.text: This stands in contrast to many clinically oriented measures of identity impairment, such as the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS; Morey, 2017), which contains many items likely to be saturated with trait negative affectivity (e.g., "My emotions rapidly shift around", "I can't even imagine living a life that I would find satisfying").
text.formatted: This stands in contrast to many clinically oriented measures of identity impairment, such as the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Morey, 2017)</ref>, which contains many items likely to be saturated with trait negative affectivity (e.g., "My emotions rapidly shift around", "I can't even imagine living a life that I would find satisfying").

text.text: Thus, the substantial overlap between measures like the SCCS and measures of trait negative affectivity cannot be straightforwardly explained by shared item content.

One possible explanation for this overlap is that difficulties maintaining a clear and coherent sense of self contribute to emotional distress; theorists have long noted that representations of the self and others are inherently intertwined with affective experience (e.g., Kernberg, 1984).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for this overlap is that difficulties maintaining a clear and coherent sense of self contribute to emotional distress; theorists have long noted that representations of the self and others are inherently intertwined with affective experience (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kernberg, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, chronic negative affectivity may undermine the stability and coherence of self-representations, such that persistent emotional distress contributes to difficulties maintaining a clear and consistent sense of identity.

Consistent with this possibility, clinical theorists have proposed that persistent emotion dysregulation may disrupt a stable sense of self, particularly when emotional experiences are intense and rapidly shifting (Linehan & Kehrer, 1993).
text.formatted: Consistent with this possibility, clinical theorists have proposed that persistent emotion dysregulation may disrupt a stable sense of self, particularly when emotional experiences are intense and rapidly shifting <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Linehan & Kehrer, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, lower self-concept clarity may not simply represent a vulnerability contributing to emotional distress but may also emerge, in part, as a consequence of chronic negative affectivity.
A third possibility is that the overlap partly reflects shared evaluative variance across global self-report measures.

Although low self-concept clarity is conceptually distinct from holding a negatively valanced self-concept (i.e., low self-esteem), such that individuals can theoretically maintain a markedly negative yet clear and consistent view of themselves, empirical research suggests that these constructs almost always covary (Campbell, 1990; Campbell et al., 1996).

text.text: Measures of both self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity may therefore reflect a general tendency to evaluate oneself in more favorable or unfavorable terms.

Thus, some of the observed association between these constructs may reflect shared evaluative content rather than equivalence in their underlying psychological processes (e.g., Biderman et al., 2018; Kallio Strand et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Thus, some of the observed association between these constructs may reflect shared evaluative content rather than equivalence in their underlying psychological processes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Biderman et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kallio Strand et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, although self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity are conceptually distinct, there are good reasons to expect overlap among their measures.

Because the two constructs are routinely used to predict the same outcomes (e.g., psychological well-being, mental health symptoms), it is important to establish how much of their predictive utility is shared versus unique.

Designs that can disentangle the temporal relations between self-concept clarity and negative affectivity would be most informative, but cross-sectional self-report assessments are easy to administer, are the most popular way to assess both constructs, and will likely remain the most common assessment approach for the foreseeable future.

Indeed, in a recent meta-analysis by Lodi- Smith and colleagues (2026) examining the overlap between selfesteem and self-concept clarity, over 90% of the included studies assessed self-concept clarity using cross-sectional self-report scales.

text.text: It is therefore valuable to subject scales of self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity to more rigorous tests of their unique predictive abilities, and examining them in relation to experiences assessed in daily life is a promising way to clarify when they capture meaningful individual differences.
Researchers have already recommended controlling for self-esteem when studying self-concept clarity, given their strong empirical overlap (Lodi-Smith et al., 2026).

text.text: The current study tests whether the same recommendation is worth extending to measures of trait negative affectivity.

The primary aim of the present study was to comprehensively examine the extent to which two theoretically distinct constructs, self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity, can be distinguished empirically.
Despite their substantial empirical overlap and shared nomological networks across psychological and interpersonal domains, prior research has yet to clearly disentangle the two.

In the current study, we tested the incremental validity of the SCCS relative to multiple operationalizations of trait negative affectivity across outcomes assessed both at baseline and in daily life.
Baseline measures were depression symptoms and overall psychological distress, outcomes that both constructs are routinely used to predict.
Outcomes from daily life comprised affective, behavioral, and interpersonal experiences, assessed over a 15-day EMA protocol.
Examining outcomes that differ in both content and method of assessment allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the two constructs' shared and distinct empirical relations.

text.text: Diagnostic Dimensions (ILIADD) study.
Participants were considered eligible to participate if they owned a study-compatible Android or iPhone smartphone and were between 18 and 50 years old.
Additionally, the sample was enriched for recent mental health treatment, with 63% reporting current or recent treatment.
Participants completed baseline questionnaires prior to a 15-day ambulatory assessment portion of the study.
All study procedures and consent were completed remotely, online.

The 15-day ambulatory assessment period following the training involved both passive sensing and ecological momentary assessment (completed via the MetricWire smartphone application) to examine how transdiagnostic psychopathology symptoms relate to social, affective and contextual outcomes.
EMA surveys included pseudo-random assessments (eight times per day) along with social interaction surveys.

Participants were instructed to complete social interaction surveys after any relevant social interactions, which were defined as direct, real-time communication lasting at least five minutes between the participant and another person.
A total of N =552 individuals completed the baseline questionnaires and ambulatory assessment protocol.

Of the total sample, 81% indicated a history of mental health treatment, with 63% indicating that they were currently in treatment (N=291) or had received mental health treatment in the past 12 months (N=55).
To ensure reliable estimates of momentary-based outcomes, participants who provided fewer than 10 ambulatory assessment observations over the 15-day period were excluded from analyses.
Thus, the final sample consisted of N=493 participants, the majority of whom were White (87%) and female (83%).
The mean age of the sample used for analyses was 30.43 years (SD = 8.68).
The HiTOP-SR (Simms et al., 2022; https://www.3plab.org/hitop) is a 405-item self-report instrument that assesses psychopathology symptoms as represented in the HiTOP model (Kotov et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The HiTOP-SR <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Simms et al., 2022</ref>; <ref type="url" target="https://www.3plab.org/hitop">https://www.3plab.org/hitop</ref>) is a 405-item self-report instrument that assesses psychopathology symptoms as represented in the HiTOP model <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kotov et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The HiTOP-SR was designed to be broad but comprehensive in scope and includes subscale and factor scales that assess a wide variety of psychopathology symptoms and behaviors.
Participants were asked to rate how much each item applied to them in the past month.
Each item was rated using a one ("Not at all") to four ("A lot") Likert scale.

Five broadbased factor scales (e.g., Distress, Emotionality), 85 specific symptom scales (e.g., Affective Lability, Depressed Mood), and 11 alcohol use scales (e.g., Craving, Hazardous Use) were computed using the HiTOP-SR items.

Our focus was on the symptom/facet scales of Depressed Mood, Anxious Worry, Shame/Guilt, Affective Lability, and Irritability, which past structural research has demonstrated as most representative of trait negative affectivity (Mostajabi et al., 2026a).

text.text: The BFI-2 (Soto & John, 2017) is a 60-item self-report measure of the Big Five personality domains.
text.formatted: The BFI-2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Soto & John, 2017)</ref> is a 60-item self-report measure of the Big Five personality domains.

text.text: Each item was rated on a one ("Disagree strongly") to five ("Agree strongly") Likert scale, with participants being asked to rate their agreement with a series of statements about themselves (e.g., "I am someone who is moody, has up and down mood swings").
Items were averaged to create mean scales for each domain, as well as mean facet scales within each domain (three facet scales for each domain).
Our analyses focused solely on the Negative Emotionality domain and its respective facets of Anxiety, Depression, and Emotional Volatility.

The SCCS (Campbell et al., 1996) is a 12-item selfreport measure designed to assess self-concept clarity, which refers to the extent that self-beliefs are stable, clear and internally consistent. (sample item: "In general, I have a clear sense of who I am and what I am").

(sample item: "In general, I have a clear sense of who I am and what I am").

text.text: Participants were asked to rate their agreement with each item using a one ("Strongly Disagree") to five ("Strongly Agree") Likert scale.
A total mean score was computed from the 12 SCCS items.
To facilitate comparison with facet scales from the BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR, the SCCS was reverse coded, such that higher values on the SCCS represented lower selfconcept clarity.
The PHQ-8 (Kroenke et al., 2009) is a brief self-report measure of depression symptoms and assesses common features of depression.
text.formatted: The PHQ-8 <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kroenke et al., 2009)</ref> is a brief self-report measure of depression symptoms and assesses common features of depression.

text.text: The PHQ-8 was administered using eight Likert scale items ranging from zero ("Not at all") to three ("Nearly every day").
Participants were asked to rate how much they had been bothered by each symptom (e.g., "Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless") in the previous two weeks.
A total score reflecting overall level of depression symptoms was computed by summing the eight items.
The K6 (Kessler et al., 2003) is a brief selfreport measure of overall psychological distress.
text.formatted: The K6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kessler et al., 2003)</ref> is a brief selfreport measure of overall psychological distress.

text.text: The K6 is comprised of six items, each rated using a zero ("None of the time") to four ("All of the time") Likert scale.
Participants were asked to rate how often they had a particular feeling (e.g., nervous, hopeless, that everything was an effort) in the past 30 days.
The total K6 score was used as an index of overall impairment, with past work demonstrating that total scores between 13-24 were indicative of a clinical degree of impairment (Kessler et al., 2003).

text.text: Momentary Affect and Stress.
During each random prompt, participants rated their mood using four items.
Positive affect was assessed with one item ("In the past 15 minutes, how POSITIVE have you felt?") using a zero ("Neutral") to ten ("Very Positive") sliding scale.
Participants also rated negative affect with one item ("In the past 15 minutes, how NEGATIVE have you felt?") using a zero ("Neutral") to ten ("Very Negative") sliding scale.
In addition to rating positive and negative affect, participants rated their momentary stress ("In the past 15 minutes, how STRESSED have you felt?").
Stress was rated using a zero ("Not at all") to ten ("Extremely") sliding scale.

We assessed impulsivity as an outcome, as individuals with low self-concept clarity experience uncertainty and inconsistency in their self-views, which may undermine effective self-regulation (Finkenauer et al., 2005; Mostajabi et al., 2026b).

text.text: Our primary analyses used multilevel structural equation models (MSEMs) to estimate the relations between baseline predictors (BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facet scales, HiTOP-SR facet scales, and the SCCS) and our selected outcome measures.

MSEM allows the overall variability in individuals' responses to be divided into between-and within-person variance components like standard multilevel modeling approaches, but also provides additional benefits, including the latent decomposition of between-and within-person variance (Sadikaj et al., 2021).
text.formatted: MSEM allows the overall variability in individuals' responses to be divided into between-and within-person variance components like standard multilevel modeling approaches, but also provides additional benefits, including the latent decomposition of between-and within-person variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Sadikaj et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: MSEM models were estimated in two steps.
In the first step, each of our primary predictors were entered independently as predictors of all primary outcomes.

In the second step, we tested MSEMs using BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets and SCCS scale as simultaneous predictors of all primary outcomes, and MSEMs including HiTOP-SR Distress facets and the SCCS as simultaneous predictors of all primary outcomes.
In total, the SCCS and trait negative affectivity scales were compared in relation to 14 outcomes.
Two outcome variables were administered at baseline (PHQ-8 and K6), and twelve outcomes were derived from the EMA protocol.

These twelve outcomes were average positive and negative affect (from random assessments and during interpersonal interactions), stress (from random assessments and during interpersonal interactions), rash action and rash inaction (from random assessments), momentary authenticity (during interpersonal interactions), and three random slopes.
The random slopes were estimated by regressing momentary stress, momentary negative affect, and momentary positive affect on momentary authenticity, all assessed during interpersonal interactions.

Random slopes allow individuals to differ in the strength of these within-person associations and allowed us to evaluate whether the strength of these within-person associations varied as a function of individual differences in our baseline predictors (i.e., a cross-level interaction).
Using the standardized effects drawn from the MSEM results described above, we also examined indices of profile similarity between the SCCS and the facets from the BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR.

We quantified profile similarity using double-entry correlations (r ICC ; Furr, 2010), which consider the shape (i.e., correlation), elevation (i.e., mean values), and scatter (i.e., variance) of the standardized regression coefficients and thus represent an index of global similarity.
Bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals were also computed to evaluate whether r ICC values significantly differed from one another.

text.text: For all other outcomes of affect and stress, reverse-coded SCCS performed similarly to the BFI facets.

After accounting for the overlap amongst the three facets of BFI-2 Negative Emotionality and SCCS, reverse-coded SCCS remained significantly related to impulsivity and authenticity during social interactions (rash action: β = .31; 95% CI = .19; .40; rash inaction: β = .29; 95% CI = .16; .40; authenticity: β = -.25; 95% CI = -.36; -.15).

BFI-2 Anxiety was the only facet that remained significantly negatively related to rash action (β = -.10; 95% CI = -.21; -.01) whereas BFI-2 Depression was the only facet that remained significantly related to authenticity (β = -.15; 95% CI = -.28; -.03).

Reverse-coded SCCS showed a comparatively large unique association, exceeded only by the Depression facet, with both the K6 (β = .22; 95% CI = .14; .28) and PHQ-8 (β = .23; 95% CI = .14; .30), though these effects were attenuated compared to its independentmodel estimates (PHQ-8: β dropped from .46 to .23; K6: β dropped from .48 to .22).
Last, there were three significant cross-level moderation effects observed in the simultaneous model that were not observed in the independent models.

These moderation effects were confined to reverse-coded SCCS and BFI-2 Emotional Volatility, where both scales significantly moderated the positive within-person effect between momentary authenticity and momentary positive affect, and BFI-2 Emotional Volatility also moderated the negative withinperson effect between momentary authenticity and negative affect.

For reverse-coded SCCS, this cross-level moderation effect was negative (β= -.20, 95% CI= -.35; -.02), meaning that after controlling for its overlap with the BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets, lower SCCS was related to a significantly weaker association between momentary authenticity and positive affect during interpersonal interactions.

For Emotional Volatility, this moderation effect was positive (β= .19, 95% CI= .02; .35), such that after controlling for overlap with reverse-coded SCCS and the other BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets, Emotional Volatility was related to a significantly stronger association between momentary authenticity and momentary positive affect during interpersonal interactions.

For the negative within-person relation between momentary authenticity and negative affect, Emotional Volatility was related to a significantly stronger negative association at the within-person level (β= -.27, 95% CI= -.41; -.13).

text.text: When the HiTOP-SR facets of Anxious Worry, Affective Lability, Irritability, Depressed Mood and Shame/Guilt were entered independently, the HiTOP-SR facets associations with the random slopes of positive affect and stress were not significant.
However, all HiTOP-SR facets were independently associated with the random slope for negative affect.
Similar to the BFI-2 models, reverse-coded SCCS showed a stronger negative effect size relative to HiTOP-SR facets when predicting authenticity (β = -.25; 95% CI = -.31; -.19).

Consistent with the BFI-2 Depression facet, the HiTOP-SR Depressed Mood facet showed the strongest associations with both the PHQ-8 (β = .69; 95% CI = .65; .71) and the K6 (β = .75; 95% CI = .71; .77).

After accounting for the shared variance between reverse-coded SCCS and the facets of the HiTOP-SR, similar to the BFI-2 simultaneous model, there was a general pattern of attenuation of effects for the reverse-coded SCCS, and for many outcomes, the 95% credible interval included zero.

However, reverse-coded SCCS was the only predictor to remain significant for momentary authenticity during social interactions (β = -.31; 95% CI = -.42; -.20), and remained related to the baseline measures of psychopathology and momentary outcomes of impulsive behavior, though these relations were smaller in magnitude (β range = .08-.19).
HiTOP-SR Affective Lability was also uniquely associated with rash action (β = .22; 95% CI = .09; .34), at a magnitude comparable to the SCCS (β = .17; 95% CI = .06; .27).

Regarding cross-level moderation effects, although the pattern of results was consistent with those observed in the models using BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets (e.g., the cross-level moderation effect of reverse-scored SCCS on the within-person effect of momentary authenticity and positive affect), there were no cross-level moderation effects observed where the 95% credible intervals excluded zero (see supplementary table 2).

text.text: To quantify the overall empirical similarity of reverse-coded SCCS and trait negative affectivity facet scales, we computed the double-entry intraclass correlation (r ICC ) between the reverse-coded SCCS's profile of standardized associations across all outcomes (drawn from the independent MSEM models) and the corresponding profiles for each BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR facet.

Across facets from both the BFI-2 (r ICCs ranging from .86 to .94) and HiTOP-SR (r ICCs ranging from .90 to .97), r ICC values showed very strong similarity, highlighting that the pattern of relations these scales showed with our study outcomes were close to identical in most cases.

text.text: The aim of the current study was to investigate the empirical distinguishability of the SCCS and facets of Negative Emotionality and trait negative affectivity derived from the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2) and the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology-Self-Report (HiTOP-SR), respectively.

Despite their theoretical distinctions, previous research has demonstrated substantial negative correlations between trait negative affectivity and self-concept clarity (Campbell et al., 1996; Connor, 2020), with associations comparable in magnitude to those observed between self-concept clarity and self-esteem, a theoretically more proximal "sibling" construct (Lodi-Smith et al., 2026; Weber et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Despite their theoretical distinctions, previous research has demonstrated substantial negative correlations between trait negative affectivity and self-concept clarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Campbell et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Connor, 2020)</ref>, with associations comparable in magnitude to those observed between self-concept clarity and self-esteem, a theoretically more proximal "sibling" construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lodi-Smith et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Weber et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, researchers have yet to comprehensively examine the extent to which the SCCS accounts for unique variance beyond trait negative affectivity and its specific facets, particularly in predicting outcomes assessed in daily life.

To address this gap, we examined the empirical similarity of these measures in relation to well-validated clinical measures of depression and psychological distress assessed at baseline (PHQ-8 and K6), as well as relevant indices derived from a 15-day EMA protocol, including authenticity, impulsivity, affect, and stress.
Reverse-coded self-concept clarity retained unique predictive validity beyond measures of trait negative affectivity.

Specifically, reverse-coded SCCS scores remained uniquely and significantly associated with PHQ-8 and K6 scores, reflecting global depression and psychological distress, as well as momentary authenticity, rash inaction, and rash action, after accounting for trait negative affectivity operationalized using both the BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR.

Reverse-coded self-concept clarity also retained unique associations with momentary stress and negative affect during interpersonal interactions, as well as general momentary stress, in models incorporating the BFI-2 operationalization of negative affectivity; however, these associations did not hold in the corresponding HiTOP-SR models.
In contrast, the SCCS demonstrated more limited incremental validity for momentary positive and negative affect, both generally and within interpersonal contexts.

Taken together, these findings suggest that although the SCCS and measures of trait negative affectivity demonstrate considerable empirical overlap, particularly in relation to affective outcomes, they are not entirely redundant.

Although the strong zero-order relations between the SCCS and our primary outcomes were partly explained by its overlap with trait negative affectivity scales, self-concept clarity appears to provide distinct predictive utility concerning momentary authenticity, impulsivity-related experiences, and global depression and psychological distress beyond trait negative affectivity.
Implications for these findings are discussed below.

The SCCS demonstrated evidence of incremental validity for the outcomes of momentary authenticity, rash inaction and rash action, and the cross-level moderation of within-person effects involving momentary authenticity and positive affect, all of which have important theoretical ties to self-concept clarity.

Remarkably, the SCCS demonstrated unique predictive abilities in relation to both the K6 and PHQ-8 operationalizations of global depression and distress, despite the inclusion of specific scales from the BFI-2 and HiTOP-SR explicitly tied to these outcomes (e.g., BFI-2-Depression).
However, these incremental effects varied across operationalizations of trait negative affectivity.
Specifically, after accounting for the HiTOP facets, the SCCS remained the sole significant predictor for momentary authenticity.
SCCS's unique association with momentary authenticity after accounting for trait negative affectivity provides useful insight into the nature of the overlap between these constructs.

Specifically, one of the items used to assess momentary authenticity, "I had a clear sense of who I was," closely resembles an item from the SCCS, "In general, I have a clear sense of who I am and what I am."

This overlap in item content provides an opportunity to examine trait-state convergence, as the association between trait self-concept clarity and momentary authenticity may reflect the extent to which individuals' stable self-concept clarity corresponds with their momentary experiences of self-understanding (Fleeson, 2001).

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with previous research demonstrating correspondence between trait-level and daily experiences of self-concept clarity (Nezlek & Plesko, 2001).

text.text: We extend these findings by clarifying the SCCS's unique association with momentary authenticity beyond trait negative affectivity suggests that this relationship is not entirely attributable to shared variance with general negative emotionality.

Additionally, the moderating role of SCCS in the association between momentary authenticity and positive affect offers further insight into its function as a psychological resource. Ellison and colleagues (2020) found that low self-concept clarity predicted impatience and state negative affect for some, but not all, individuals, supporting the conceptualization of self-concept clarity as a psychological resource that facilitates behavioral and emotional regulation (Campbell, 1996).

text.text: Our findings help clarify this heterogeneity by suggesting that the psychological resource function of self-concept clarity may be specific to individuals with higher levels of self-concept clarity.

Specifically, self-concept clarity moderated the within-person association between state authenticity and positive affect, such that higher self-concept clarity was associated with a stronger positive relationship between momentary authenticity and positive affect.

This moderation did not extend to stronger decreases in negative affect when reporting higher momentary authenticity, suggesting that self-concept clarity may function as a resource that amplifies the positive affective benefits of authentic self-expression among individuals who possess higher levels of self-concept clarity.
In addition, the SCCS showed incremental validity when predicting rash inaction after accounting for both the HiTOP-SR and BFI-2 facets.

These findings support Kashyap and Lal's (2026) hypothesis that self-concept clarity may function as a psychological resource for impulse control and suggest that impulsive behavior is a function of both identity-related processes and trait negative affectivity.

text.text: Indeed, SCCS's unique association with rash action remained significant after accounting for both operationalizations of trait negative affectivity.
In the HiTOP-SR model, however, Affective Lability was also uniquely associated with rash action, and its association was comparable in magnitude to that of the SCCS.

This suggests that, when trait negative affectivity is assessed more comprehensively as opposed to a general domain score, individual facets such as Affective Lability may account for as much of the association with rash action as self-concept clarity does.

Thus, the incremental validity observed for the SCCS in the BFI-2 models compared to the HiTOP-SR models may partly reflect differences in breadth across the two operationalizations and suggests that different measures may produce different results regarding incremental utility of self-concept clarity relative to trait negative affectivity.

For example, NEO-based instruments of neuroticism include facet scales of Self-consciousness and Vulnerability (Costa & McCrae, 1995), which do not have direct analogues in the facets we investigated here, and may provide further insight into areas of overlap between self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity.

text.text: Moreover, the differing patterns across rash action and rash inaction are consistent with the view that impulsivity is a multifaceted construct (e.g., Carver & Johnson, 2018) and with recent work suggesting that it may be useful to distinguish between active and inactive components (Mostajabi et al., 2026b, preprint).

text.text: The present findings extend this literature by suggesting that rash inaction may be more closely related to identity functioning, whereas rash action may be more closely associated with trait negative affectivity, particularly affective lability.

Future research should examine the differential associations of rash action and rash inaction with identity constructs and trait negative affectivity to further clarify the distinct nomological networks of these impulsivity components.

The retention of unique predictive utility for self-concept clarity across two operationalizations of depressive symptoms and psychological distress (the PHQ-8 and K6), even after accounting for facets of trait negative affectivity, is particularly noteworthy given the well-established associations between negative affectivity and depressive symptoms (e.g., Kotov et al., 2010 , Lakhtakia et al, 2024), as well as the inherently distressing nature of negative emotional experiences.

text.text: These findings suggest that the coherence and stability of one's selfconcept account for unique variance in depression and psychological distress beyond individual differences in the tendency to experience negative affect.

Thus, although self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity are empirically related, their associations with depressive symptoms and psychological distress are not entirely reducible to the same underlying construct.

The limited incremental validity of SCCS beyond trait negative affectivity in predicting momentary outcomes of positive and negative affect, and the shared variation found across all outcomes points to important empirical overlap between these two constructs that should be considered in future research contexts.

Specifically, it is important for researchers attempting to capture identity disturbance using the SCCS to account for its overlap with trait negative affectivity and take deliberate steps to parse variance distinct to identity disturbance from that attributable to broader negative affectivity.

Indeed, in their recent meta-analysis, Lodi-Smith and colleagues (2026) found a correlation of r = .65 between self-esteem and self-concept clarity and in turn argued that it was critical to assess both constructs in studies on either self-esteem or selfconcept clarity to provide a more precise characterization of each.

Our findings dovetail nicely with their recommendations and are worth emphasizing given the present findings-the pattern of correlations between the SCCS and most trait negative affectivity scales are on par with the correlation between self-esteem and self-concept clarity.
Importantly, this does not mean researchers can make clear, unambiguous inferences after controlling for trait negative affectivity in analyses of self-concept clarity.
As cautioned by Lynam and colleagues (2006; see also Hoyle et al., 2023), researchers must consider what remains of a construct after controlling for highly correlated neighboring constructs.
text.formatted: As cautioned by <ref type="bibr">Lynam and colleagues (2006</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hoyle et al., 2023)</ref>, researchers must consider what remains of a construct after controlling for highly correlated neighboring constructs.

text.text: For example, if aspects of trait negative affectivity contribute to lower self-concept clarity, then statistically controlling for trait negative affectivity in an effort to self-concept clarity would lead to meaningful components of self-concept clarity being partialed out.

Alternatively, if they are not constitutive of one another (e.g., they covary because of a general negative evaluative tendency), controlling for trait negative affectivity may be useful for determining whether associations attributed to self-concept clarity are better explained by a broader tendency to experience negative emotions, and vice versa.
Given the nuanced pattern of our findings, it is likely that these constructs are partly, but not fully, constitutive of one another.

Therefore, researchers will benefit from using multiple analytic approaches, including zero-order associations alongside unique associations to appropriately contextualize findings and ensure that associations attributed to self-concept clarity are interpreted alongside the substantial variance it shares with trait negative affectivity (and vice versa).
Results should be interpreted with several limitations in mind.
First, the present sample is primarily White (87%) and majority female (83%) which affects the generalizability of our findings.

Given that women have been found to exhibit lower levels of self-concept clarity and that self-concept clarity has been found to differ across Western and Eastern cultures (Campbell et al., 1996), research is needed to investigate whether our findings generalize across other populations and sociocultural contexts.

text.text: Second, although the SCCS developed by Campbell and colleagues (1996) is a widely used and well-validated measure of self-concept clarity, the use of alternative measures of this construct may have yielded different results (e.g., Burger & Guadagno, 2003; Hamid & Cheng, 1995; Slotter et al., 2010).

text.text: Additionally, the SCCS captures a relatively narrow aspect of identity functioning.

Measures that assess other dimensions of self-belief, such as identity disturbance (Self-Concept and Identity Measure; SCIM; Kaufman et al., 2015), self-esteem (Rosenberg, 1965), or self-efficacy (Chen et al., 2001), may demonstrate different patterns of predictive utility across the outcomes examined.

text.text: Given longstanding concerns about construct proliferation in the self-belief literature (Marsh et al., 2019), future research should investigate the empirical distinctiveness of trait negative affectivity from a broader range of measures of identity functioning and self-beliefs.

text.text: Additionally, both self-concept clarity and affective instability (i.e., the HiTOP affective lability facet) were conceptualized and assessed at the trait level.

Given theoretical perspectives suggesting that impairments in the unity and coherence of the self-concept may contribute to affective instability and negative affect (Horowitz, 1977; Kernberg, 1975; Stein, 1995), it is plausible that the SCCS's limited incremental predictive utility for affective outcomes beyond the affective lability facet reflects, in part, the difficulty of disentangling their potentially interrelated processes using exclusively trait-level measures.

text.text: If difficulties in maintaining a coherent selfconcept contribute to affective instability, these constructs may be difficult to distinguish when assessed as relatively stable individual differences.
Future research should therefore investigate how self-concept clarity and affective instability relate to one another and to affective outcomes using measures collected over shorter timescales.
Such approaches may help clarify the temporal dynamics linking difficulties in maintaining a coherent self-concept with fluctuations in affective experience.

Although the present study included adults ranging from 18 to 50 years of age, thereby extending prior self-concept clarity research beyond the adolescent and young adult samples typical in this line of work, this broader age range may have also weakened some associations.
Identity development is particularly salient during adolescence and young adulthood, when individuals experience substantial identity exploration and life transitions.
Consequently, selfconcept clarity may play a more prominent role in daily emotional and identity functioning during this developmental period than in adulthood.

Future research should therefore examine the incremental validity of self-concept clarity beyond broader measures of negative affectivity within adolescent and young adult samples to determine whether the present pattern of findings generalizes to populations in which identity development is most active.

Overall, the SCCS and trait negative affectivity demonstrated unique associations with momentary authenticity, impulsivity, and global measures of depression and psychological distress, above and beyond their shared variance; however, the SCCS's associations with momentary affective experiences were more limited, with much of its relation to these outcomes attributable to its shared variance with trait negative affectivity.
These findings provide evidence that, despite their considerable overlap, the two constructs retain distinct associations with several important aspects of psychological functioning.

Given these nuanced findings, researchers using the SCCS to investigate identity-related functioning and psychological wellbeing should consider its overlap with trait negative affectivity and take deliberate steps to distinguish variance uniquely attributable to self-concept clarity from that shared with broader negative emotionality.
This work provides a valuable step towards further clarifying the relationship between self-concept clarity and trait negative affectivity.
